data.description:
## Symptom

`tests/unit/test_fetch_common_dir_coordination.py::test_uncoordinated_parallel_fetches_can_race_but_coordination_prevents_it`
failed in a full `make verify` on a heavily loaded host (two concurrent `make verify` runs,
each `-n 4 --dist worksteal`). It passes in ordinary runs.

Failure point, from the run log:

```
tests/unit/test_fetch_common_dir_coordination.py:431: AssertionError
```

Line 431 is:

```python
assert observed, "expected the uncoordinated parallel fetches to race git's ref CAS"
```

## This is the CONTROL arm, not the coordination arm

The test has two halves:

- Lines 426–431 — the control: run up to 40 uncoordinated rounds and assert that a ref-CAS
  race **was observed at least once**.
- Lines 433–436 — the subject: run 8 coordinated rounds and assert **zero** races.

The failure is in the first. The coordination lock under test is not implicated: the suite
never reached the assertion that checks it. Nothing here suggests `fetch_coordination_lock`
is broken.

## Why it fails

The control asserts that a race **will** occur. Its own comment states the assumption:

```python
# Observe the race WITHOUT coordination. High base rate → a small cap is more than
# enough; hitting the cap with zero races would itself be astronomically unlikely.
```

That "astronomically unlikely" holds only while the 6 worker threads actually overlap. They
synchronize on a `threading.Barrier(n)` and then each runs a real `git fetch`. On a saturated
host the threads release from the barrier and are then descheduled far enough apart that the
fetches serialize, so git's ref CAS never collides and `observed` stays 0 through all 40
rounds.

So the base rate is not a constant of the code — it is a function of host load, and the test
treats it as a constant. Under contention the assumption inverts: serialization becomes the
likely outcome, not the astronomically unlikely one.

## Why it matters

It is a false negative that costs a full re-run: the test reports a failure when the
production code is fine and the host was merely busy. Multiple agent sessions share this
host and routinely run concurrent verifies, so the loaded condition is normal here, not
exotic. Per project rule a flaky test is a bug to root-cause, not something to retry.

## Direction (not prescriptive)

The control arm is trying to prove the lock is load-bearing — that without it the race is
real. That is worth keeping, but it should not be established by racing live threads and
hoping. Options worth weighing: drive the uncoordinated case deterministically rather than
probabilistically, or separate the "the race exists" evidence from the per-run assertion so a
busy host cannot manufacture a failure. Whatever is chosen must still fail if the
coordination lock stops working — a fix that makes the test pass unconditionally is not a fix.

## Explicitly NOT this bug

The same run also failed two CLI facade tests on a stale stderr logging handler. That is a
different cause in a different file and is tracked separately as `cded-334b-a742-4082`
(bald-diagnostic-cricket). Diagnosing them together would conflate two unrelated defects.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The test no longer fails when the host is saturated: it passes while two concurrent
      `make verify`-scale workloads run on the same machine.
- [ ] The test still FAILS if the coordination lock is defeated — demonstrated by disabling
      or stubbing `fetch_coordination_lock` and showing a red result. A test that cannot fail
      has not been fixed.
- [ ] The evidence that uncoordinated fetches race is preserved somewhere durable, not merely
      deleted to make the red go away.
- [ ] `make verify` passes.

## Provider neutrality

Pure local git and Python threading. No CI provider, model or vendor is involved, so the fix
behaves the same under any CI provider or none.
data.title: Fetch-coordination control arm asserts a race that a loaded host can prevent
